summary: This document describes a way to send a single aggregated status message for many statically configured pseudowires on one MPLS label switched path. This reduces the amount of refresh signaling needed to keep track of whether each pseudowire is working.

eli5.summary: Instead of calling every friend one by one to say you are okay, you send one group message that covers everybody.

subtitle: One aggregated keepalive per LSP lets static pseudowires stop sending their own periodic status refreshes.

tldr.problem: Statically configured pseudowires need their status tracked, but periodic status messages for each PW on a busy LSP can overwhelm the network.
tldr.mechanism: The PEs run a small keepalive-style protocol per LSP over the Generic Associated Channel. Once it is ACTIVE, individual PW status messages can use a Refresh Timer of zero, because the LSP-level session covers them.
tldr.outcome: Far fewer messages are needed, a remote PE restart is detected, and an optional configuration message can detect provisioning mismatches.

today: RFC 8237 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2017. It has not been obsoleted or updated according to the metadata for this site.

sections.title: Why Reduce PW Status Refreshes
sections.content:
Pseudowires (PWs) over an MPLS network are set up with static label assignment (RFC 8077), and their status is carried as described in RFC 6478. That RFC offers two modes: periodic retransmission of non-zero status messages, or a simple acknowledgment of PW status. This document applies when status is acknowledged immediately with a requested refresh value of zero, meaning no refresh.

The RFC gives four reasons for the protocol: it greatly improves scalability by reducing the messages a Provider Edge (PE) must send periodically, it detects a remote PE restart, a PE that lost local state can request a status refresh, and it can optionally detect a remote provisioning change.
sections.eli5: If every toy in a toy box had to shout 'I am still here' every few seconds, it would be very noisy. One lookout for the whole box is much quieter.

sections.title: The Protocol and Its States
sections.content:
The protocol is a simple message sent at the LSP level over the MPLS Generic Associated Channel (G-ACh, RFC 5586). A PE MUST send the message as soon as a PW is configured on the LSP, then retransmit it at a locally configured interval given in the Refresh Timer field. This timer has no relationship to the individual PW status Refresh Timers.

There are three states. INACTIVE is entered when the protocol is turned off or all PWs on the LSP are deprovisioned. In STARTUP the PE sends periodic messages with Ack Session ID set to 0 until it receives one carrying its own Session ID. ACTIVE is entered when such a message arrives within 3.5 times the Refresh Timer of the last message sent.

ACTIVE falls back to STARTUP if no valid message arrives within 3.5 times the Refresh Timer, or if a message arrives with a wrong or zero Ack Session ID. It goes to INACTIVE if all PWs are deprovisioned or the protocol is disabled.

To change the timer while ACTIVE, the PE sends a message with the new value. A larger value takes effect immediately. A smaller value takes effect after 3.5 times the original value, or at the first valid message received. The receiver acknowledges the new value immediately.
sections.eli5: Two friends keep tossing a ball back and forth. If the ball keeps coming back in time, everything is fine. If it stops coming back, they start over.

sections.title: Refresh Reduction Procedure
sections.content:
While the protocol is ACTIVE on an LSP, the PE can send all PW status messages for PWs on that LSP with a Refresh Timer of zero. Once a PW status message is acknowledged, repeating it is unnecessary. To reach ACTIVE quickly, before the first PW status Refresh Timer expires, the refresh reduction timer should be much smaller than the PW status timer.

If the session ends by entering INACTIVE or STARTUP, the PE MUST immediately resend all previously sent PW status messages for that LSP. The Refresh Timer MUST NOT be zero then, and follows local policy. Implementations MUST avoid flooding the remote PE, and for administrative terminations where the remote PE is still reachable, SHOULD pace the transmission.
sections.eli5: If the lookout goes quiet, everyone has to speak up again, but they should take turns instead of shouting all at once.

sections.title: Message Encoding
sections.content:
The message follows the LSP label stack entry and the G-ACh Label (GAL). Its fixed header carries a Session ID, an Ack Session ID, a Refresh Timer and a Total Message Length. The Session ID is a non-zero, locally selected number that is not preserved if the PE restarts. A CRC-16 over the date and time is a recommended way to pick one.

The Refresh Timer is a non-zero unsigned 16-bit value, at least 10, in milliseconds. The default of 30000 is RECOMMENDED. Total Message Length counts the Checksum, Message Type, Flags, Message Sequence Number and Control Message Body. Zero means no control message follows.

The remaining fields are optional: Checksum, Message Sequence Number, Last Received Sequence Number, Message Type, the flags and the body. If an optional field is included, all optional fields before it MUST be included. The Message Sequence Number starts at 1 when ACTIVE is entered, wraps back to 1, and 0 MUST NOT be used.

The U flag governs unknown messages or TLVs. If U is 0, a notification with code 0x4 is sent and the session returns to STARTUP. If U is 1, the item is acknowledged and silently ignored. The C flag marks the end of configuration transmission. The other 6 flag bits MUST be 0 on transmission and ignored on reception.
sections.eli5: Each message has a little envelope with a session number, a timer, and a length. Extra notes can be tucked inside, but only if the envelope says they are there.

sections.title: Control Messages and Configuration Checks
sections.content:
Control messages always piggyback on normal refresh reduction messages, with one control message per message. If one is not acknowledged within 3.5 times the Refresh Timer, a fatal notification, 'Unacknowledged control message', MUST be sent and the session terminated.

The Notification message (type 0x01) mostly acknowledges receipt by echoing the sequence number. Its 32-bit Notification Code of 0 is a 'Null Notification'. Error codes force the session back to STARTUP.

The PW Configuration message (type 0x02) is optional and carries sub-TLVs: the MPLS-TP Tunnel ID (type 0x01, 20 octets, sent at least once), a PW ID Configured List (0x02) and a PW ID Unconfigured List (0x03), each holding up to 8 PW Path IDs of 32 octets. The sender sets the C bit on the last such message. Listing the same PW in both lists is a fatal error.

A PE that receives configuration it will not process answers with 'PW configuration not supported'. If it finds a PW configured locally but not remotely, it SHOULD treat the PW as 'Not Forwarding', set the attachment circuit status to reflect the fault, and raise an alarm. It MUST send a 'PW configuration mismatch' notification. After a new PW is added, verification of it MUST be held for at least 30 seconds.
sections.eli5: Besides saying 'still here', the two ends can compare lists of who they think is connected, and complain if the lists do not match.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The RFC says the security considerations of RFC 6478 are adequate, since the operating environment is almost identical. The protocol is designed for two adjacent PEs joined by a physical link, so traffic cannot be misdirected or injected without compromising the PW transport link itself.

IANA created registries for message types, configuration sub-TLVs, 32-bit notification codes (0 through 7 defined here, with an Error? column) and message flags. It also allocated G-ACh channel type 0x29 for PW Status Refresh Reduction.
sections.eli5: The two ends are right next to each other on one wire, so a stranger cannot slip in a fake note without breaking into that wire.
